newsitem.title: UAE: FEATURE - German camel diplomacy in UAE desert.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - German camel diplomacy in UAE desert.

text.p: Nine camels trotted along a dirt track in the Arabian desert as men in flowing robes waved thin canes in the air and chanted traditional poems.

United Arab Emirates President Sheikh Zaid bin Sultan al-Nahayan and some of his sons clapped and inspected each beast from a viewing stand as a small army of bodyguards with automatic weapons stood by.

But this was no ordinary camel race. The jockeys straddling the lumbering animals were mostly German women with blonde hair. And the audience that included a German parliamentarian and businessmen even cheered the camel that crossed the finish line last -- without a jockey.
"I call it camel diplomacy," said Hans-Joachim Fuchtel, a parliamentarian who is leading a 220-strong German delegation visiting this Gulf Arab state of fabulous oil wealth.
"In the 60's ping-pong helped the U.S. and China. For us it's camels. I am sure this will help business and trade between Germany and the UAE," he added.
Thirty German riders are training in the vast deserts of the UAE to become camel jockeys in time for Europe's first camel race to be held this summer.
DIEHARD CAMEL RACING FANS
Many UAE citizens -- from Sheikh Zaid and top business executives to the young boys who live in small cement block homes on the edge of the track -- are diehard camel racing fans.
And across the closed, conservative societies of the Gulf, Western businessmen sometimes struggle in vain for months or years to meet the right people.
"This (camel race) was a door opener to the highest people in the state," said German parliament member Steffen Kampeter.

"We would not get this during normal government meetings," he added after the race as he watched some of Sheikh Zaid's guards piling into a Mercedes, a common sight in this country of eight-lane highways and gleaming skyscrapers.
CAMELS TO BOOST TOURISM IN GERMANY

Fuchtel is banking on the camel, known as the ship of the desert for its ability to travel long distances, to eventually arouse passions among Germans and draw tourists to his home constituency in the Black Forest region.
Europe's only camel farm is in the small southern German town of Rotfelden, part of Fuchtel's political domain. Set up 10 years ago, it is now home to 80 camels.
Fuchtel hopes the camel race to be held this summer in Berlin, Munich or the southern German spa town of Baden-Baden is only the beginning.
"People asked me 'Are you mad? What's wrong with your brain?'" Fuchtel said. "I told them that 200 or 300 years ago, Germany started importing potatoes," now a main staple of German cuisine.
$1 MILLION CAMELS
A top racing camel used for breeding purposes can cost as much as $1 million. But so far, importing camels has not been too costly for Germany.
After hearing about the unique farm, Sheikh Zaid last year gave Germany 19 racing camels which were transported on a special large-cabin cargo plane.
And after the al-Wathba race on January 6, he donated the farm another 26 camels.
A UAE official at the race said Sheikh Zaid also gave the farm 100 million marks ($64 million) as an annual subsidy. It was not clear for how many years the subsidy would be paid.
BUMPY RIDE
The German camel-jockeys were recruited from sports colleges and riding schools and have been training in the UAE for three weeks.
"We were scared that the camels would move very fast," said 41-year-old Renate Vialle, a social worker who is learning to become a jockey with her 16-year-old daughter.
"In the first days it was just too much. It was too hard training on the track. People had trouble breathing because it was bumpy," she added.

But Mohammad Ahmadou, one of their Mauritanian instructors, said there was hope, despite the language barriers -- he can only communicate in French to a few of the students who must translate for the rest.
During the first few days of training, he led the fledgling camel-jockeys on a 30-km (20-mile) desert trek, constantly urging them to alter their pace and understand their mounts.
"I thought they would fall but they didn't. You tell them something once and they listen. These people are serious," he said, as he pointed to his best students.
So are the German business executives visiting the UAE.

So far, they have had about 200 appointments with local business leaders to explore opportunities beyond the 2.43 billion marks in luxury German cars, machinery and electrical goods that were exported to the UAE in 1995.
"This camel racing is a good bridge for business," said Hans Digel, owner of a clothing company in the Black Forest.
